stories.headline: Mamdani handed out $95K in staff raises the same day he warned of $12B budget deficit: report
stories.note: NYC's socialist mayor hands his staff raises while warning of a $12B hole, a gift to GOP messaging on Democrat spending.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has signed off on roughly $850,000 in raises for at least 46 City Hall aides since taking office in January, according to payroll records first reviewed by the New York Post.

The timing is drawing the most attention: on Jan. 28, five staffers got bumps worth a combined $95,000 on the very day Mamdani told the city it faced an estimated $12 billion budget gap. His office later revised that projection down to about $5.4 billion.

Two aides, Julia Simcoe and Jacob Russell, each saw raises of more than $60,000, lifting their pay to $148,000 and $145,000. The Post also counted 21 new hires who got raises before their first year was up, more than twice the combined number under Eric Adams and Bill de Blasio.

Meanwhile, the city's fiscal 2027 budget has grown by $3.3 billion since June to $129.2 billion, while key Mamdani promises like free buses, universal childcare and city-run grocery stores face cost overruns, waitlists and skepticism.
Fox News Digital asked City Hall to explain the early raises and the Jan. 28 timing; a spokesperson did not immediately respond.

Why it matters: Handing staff fat raises while warning of a deficit is exactly the kind of contrast Republicans will use to argue that socialist governance means bigger budgets and fewer results for taxpayers.

stories.headline: Texas attorney general-elect refuses to defend Ten Commandments classroom law
stories.note: Texas' incoming AG won't defend a law voters' representatives passed, handing Republicans a clear values contrast.
body: Texas Attorney General-elect Nathan Johnson, the first Democrat to win the office in nearly 30 years, says he will not defend the state law requiring the Ten Commandments to be displayed in public school classrooms.

Johnson told The Dallas Morning News the law, Senate Bill 10, is unconstitutional in his view. "I'm the one who says what the state's position is," he said, adding it won't be the position the state took before.

The law, championed by outgoing Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton and passed by the GOP-led Legislature, was upheld by the 5th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in April. The Supreme Court is now weighing whether to take up a challenge.

Paxton's office is already using Johnson's stance as an argument: in a filing this month, it told the justices they should decline the case because Johnson's office may not mount a real defense. If the high court passes, the 5th Circuit ruling in the law's favor stands.
Johnson's win was part of a broader Democratic sweep in Texas that included the Senate and governor's races.

Why it matters: A newly elected Democrat refusing to defend a law passed by the Legislature gives Republicans an early, clear-cut fight over faith and the rule of law, and Paxton may still lock in the win before he leaves in January.

stories.headline: Socialist newcomers’ old words take new turn as they prepare to enter Congress
stories.note: The incoming socialist freshmen's past statements are resurfacing, giving the GOP ammunition before they're even sworn in.
body: As a new class of Democratic Socialists of America-aligned lawmakers gets ready to be sworn in this January, Fox News Digital reviewed past comments that could follow them into committee fights and caucus politics.

New York's Darializa Avila Chevalier, who beat longtime Rep. Adriano Espaillat in a Mamdani-backed primary, once posted that abolishing the police meant "no more police at all ever," wrote "seize the means of production," and cursed out Kamala Harris. She says those posts no longer reflect who she is.
Colorado's Melat Kiros called both 9/11 and the Oct. 7 attacks on Israel "inevitable," has accused Israel of genocide, and supports abolishing ICE.

Pennsylvania's Chris Rabb told Sean Hannity he "absolutely" backs ending cash bail and a wealth tax, while saying he'd make an exception to his anti-incarceration views for people he called "MAGA thugs." New York's Claire Valdez called ICE a "militarized terrorist organization" and floated nationalizing the airline industry.
None of the four responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.
Why it matters: These incoming members hand Republicans a ready-made record on defunding police and abolishing ICE, and they create a headache for Democratic leaders trying to keep a moderate image.

stories.headline: Mamdani's top 4 socialist promises met with reality checks as his first year in office nears its end
stories.note: Mamdani's signature socialist pledges are running into reality, a cautionary tale Republicans can point to nationwide.
body: Nearly a year into his term, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani has started acting on his signature socialist promises, but each has come up smaller than advertised, according to a Fox News Digital review.

His rent freeze did happen, with the Rent Guidelines Board approving 0% increases on one- and two-year leases. But it covers only about 1 million rent-stabilized units, roughly 41% of the city's rentals.

The city-run grocery store pilot drew complaints of long lines, shortages and disorganization when it launched in February. Mamdani still wants five stores selling at 30% below market, which economists question without heavy taxpayer subsidies.

Universal childcare launched only for 2-year-olds in select neighborhoods: about 2,000 seats for more than 5,700 applicants, leaving roughly 3,700 kids on waitlists. The Independent Budget Office says an expanded version would cost about $425 million by 2028.

Free buses have stalled at the state level. Gov. Kathy Hochul said she can't pull fare revenue from the MTA, and the IBO put the cost at about $1.1 billion versus the campaign's $700 million estimate.
Why it matters: Mamdani's first year is becoming a real-world test of socialist promises, and the gap between the pitch and the results gives Republicans a powerful case to make nationally.

stories.headline: Biden book sales lag way behind Obama, Clinton memoirs in first week
stories.note: Biden's memoir is flopping next to Obama's and Clinton's, another sign Democrats' old guard has lost its pull.
body: Former President Joe Biden's new memoir, "Promise Me, America," sold just 21,000 copies in its first week, according to market research firm Circana.

That's a tiny fraction of his predecessors: Barack Obama's "A Promised Land" sold over 800,000 copies in its first day and 1 million by the end of its first week, and Bill Clinton's "My Life" hit 1 million in two weeks.

The book still reached No. 1 on the New York Times nonfiction list, and publisher Little, Brown and Company said it was "immensely proud." Biden has done no public promotion stops, citing his prostate cancer diagnosis, compared with more than 30 for his earlier memoir "Promise Me, Dad," which sold over 300,000 copies.
Jill Biden's June memoir also underperformed compared with books by other former first ladies.
Why it matters: The weak sales are another sign that public interest in the Biden era has faded fast, even among Democrats, as the party looks for new faces heading into 2028.

stories.headline: Dems plan to use new Congressional majority to relitigate Jan. 6 attack — despite citizens voting for lower costs
stories.note: Democrats look set to spend their new majority on Jan. 6 instead of costs, a gift to Republicans heading toward 2028.
body: After campaigning on lowering costs, Democrats taking over Congress are already preparing to put the Jan. 6 Capitol attack back in the spotlight, the New York Post reports.

The incoming majority is staffing investigative committees with former Justice Department prosecutors who worked Jan. 6 cases, plans to formally mark the anniversary, and wants legislation blocking taxpayer money from going to defendants Trump pardoned.
Rep. Jamie Raskin said Democrats want to keep the historical record from being rewritten, and Rep. Joe Morelle plans to move a plaque honoring Capitol police officers to a more visible spot.

The White House hit back. "Instead of working to improve the lives of Americans, Democrats want to continue their obsession with January 6," spokesperson Lauren Bis told The Post, pointing to the border, drug prices and workers' paychecks.

Related court fights, including a lawsuit by lawmakers and officers that could reach trial in 2028, and state cases against Trump allies in Arizona, Nevada and Wisconsin, could keep the topic in the news for years.
Why it matters: If Democrats spend their new majority on Jan. 6 hearings instead of affordability, Republicans get an easy argument that the party isn't delivering what voters asked for.

stories.headline: Nithya Raman’s inauguration comes with a $100K price tag for top-tier VIP access
stories.note: LA's progressive mayor-elect is selling $100K VIP access to her inauguration, an easy hypocrisy hit for the GOP.
body: Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman, a democratic socialist, is offering donors VIP inauguration packages costing up to $100,000, according to an invitation obtained by the California Post.

The top tier buys 16 reserved seats at the Dec. 13 swearing-in plus eight passes to a private reception with a photo op. Packages at $50,000 and $25,000 offer fewer seats and passes, and business contributions will be considered case by case.

The money goes to "The People's Mayor Inaugural Fund." Because the donations are filed as behested payments, they face no contribution limits under state law, though gifts of $5,000 or more must be disclosed.
Outgoing Mayor Karen Bass's team said she didn't offer similar donor packages in 2022. The Post reached out to Raman for comment.

Raman takes office inheriting a budget crisis and an estimated 45,194 homeless people, including 29,115 unsheltered, and has promised to cut tent encampments at least in half before the 2028 Olympics.
Why it matters: A self-described socialist selling six-figure VIP access to big donors is an easy hypocrisy story for Republicans, especially as LA struggles with homelessness and its budget.
